# Write a mapper

You are writing a deterministic mapper from one source system's FOLIO record items into the consumer's app views in `in/views/views.d.ts`.

## What you have (all under `in/`)

- `in/schema/homelog-v1.d.ts`: the source system's schema. This is the only documentation of the source.
  Its docstrings say what every field and code means; read all of it.
- `in/views/`: the target view definitions, written by the consumer. Their docstrings are the
  specification of the output: which rows to emit, which to leave out, units, statuses, time rules.
- `in/samples/`: 8 sample items from 2 patients of this source, in FOLIO Markdown form
  (frontmatter = envelope, then narrative, then the `json payload` block). `in/samples/samples.json` has
  the same items in JSON form, grouped by patient: that is the form your function receives.
- `in/harness/`: `sh in/harness/check.sh [asOf]` type-checks your mapper (strict, no Node/Bun types) and runs
  it on the sample patients, printing the rows.

## The task

Write `out/transform.ts` exporting

```ts
export function transform(items: FolioItem[], asOf: string): ViewRows
```

(the type `Transform` in `in/views/views.d.ts`). It receives every item this source
published for ONE patient, in no particular order, including items that were later superseded or
retracted, and a local date `asOf` (`YYYY-MM-DD`). It returns the rows describing this source's record
as of the end of that day.

Your mapper will be run, unchanged, on many other patients of this source whose records contain
situations the samples do not show. Rely on the schema's documentation for those, not only on the
samples. Nobody will review the output by hand; a mapper that runs cleanly but reads a field wrongly
produces wrong clinical data.

## Rules

- `out/transform.ts` is self-contained TypeScript. Its only allowed import is
  `import type { … } from "../in/views/views"` (and `"../in/views/views"`). No other imports.
- Deterministic: no clock (`Date.now()`, `new Date()` without an argument), no randomness, no network, no
  file system, no environment. Parsing dates with `Date.parse`/`new Date(string)` and `Intl` time-zone
  formatting are fine.
- It must type-check (`sh in/harness/check.sh`) and must not throw on input it does not expect: skip
  what it cannot read.
- You may write and run your own tests or scratch scripts under `out/` with `bun`. Only
  `out/transform.ts` is used.

When you are done, reply with a few lines on the judgment calls you made.

content.text:
I've written `out/transform.ts`. It passes the type check, gives sensible rows on both sample patients at several `asOf` dates, and handled a set of made-up edge cases correctly. That covered the cutoff at the end of a Chicago day on the date the clocks change, mmol/L and HI readings, a typed duplicate of a cuff reading, a retracted day page, paused and stopped medicines, and brand-name lookup. HomeLog has no problem, allergy or lab data, so those lists are always empty; home glucose goes in vitals.

The judgment calls:

- **Which items count:** I use only items recorded by the end of the `asOf` day in Chicago time. Anything named in an in-scope item's `supersedes` or `retracts` is dropped, even if the item doing the dropping was itself later retracted, as the rules state. The medication list comes only from the latest saved My Medicines list. For each day I keep only the latest day page, because each one restates the whole day.
- **Glucose units:** I convert each reading using its own `unit`, not the diary note about changing the meter setting. A reading whose value can't exist in its stated unit (under 20 or over 600 mg/dL, or under 1.1 or over 33.3 mmol/L, with no HI/LO flag) is skipped rather than guessed. HI/LO rows report the meter's limit converted to mg/dL.
- **Duplicate readings:** a typed reading is dropped when a device reading of the same kind has the same values and was taken within 10 minutes; the device copy is kept.
- **Times:** readings are reported exactly as written on the phone, with no shift.
- **Drug names:** the ingredient comes from the drug-search result when the patient picked one, otherwise from a built-in brand-to-generic table and a list of known generics. If a typed name isn't in either ("water pill"), the ingredient is left out. The RxNorm ingredient code is set only when the search result was ingredient-level (no strength or form in its name).
- **Conflicting strengths:** where the patient's typed strength and the picked product's strength differ only by an mg/mcg slip (levothyroxine typed as "75 mg" but picked as 0.075 mg), I trust the picked product, giving 75 mcg. Any other disagreement leaves the dose out. A dose range like "1 or 2" also leaves it out.
- **Dose and frequency:** a direction with no count ("morning") means one tablet, and I multiply the count by the per-tablet strength. Insulin, liquids and inhalers need an explicit amount. Frequency comes from the times of day mentioned. Phrases like "for my knee" count as as-needed, so the naproxen sample is as-needed with no dose.
- **Status:** a "taking" medicine whose note says it's paused (e.g. "doctor told me to stop for now") becomes "held". So does a "stopped" one whose note implies resuming ("until after…"). The stop reason is chosen by keyword matching on the note, and the note itself is kept as the reason text.
- **Same drug listed twice:** only the entry with the latest start or stop date is kept; on a tie, the one still being taken wins.
- **Sensitivity:** I mark it only for drugs that plainly belong to a category (antidepressants and antipsychotics, opioid-use treatments, contraceptives, HIV drugs). Drugs with other common uses, such as bupropion or duloxetine, are left unmarked.
- **No allergy rows:** a medicine stopped for a side effect shows up as a stopped medication with that reason, not as an allergy. HomeLog has no allergy list or diagnoses, so producing allergy rows would be inferring.

The weakest spots are the brand/generic tables and the keyword rules that read free-text notes. They're broad but not complete, so unusual names or wording will come out with less detail: no ingredient, dose, frequency or stop reason.
